text: This video is a request to Dan Mlelen.
>> All right, let's see it.
>> Will you break down the prodigal son
story as it relates to what's happening
now with aranged parents and their adult
children who have gone no contact? What
I'm seeing as a marriage and family
therapist is these aranged parents
weaponizing that story of the prodigal
son to not do any of their own self-work
or take accountability, but to further
scapegoat their children as the problem
and even social media and therapists as
if it's all some conspiracy against
parents. And so I'm really wondering
what your interpretation is of that
story as it relates to parents and their
adult children nowadays and what people
really should be taking away from that
story.
>> Hey, thank you for a great question. I
think that reading is problematic for a
few different reasons. We can start with
the name of the parable. The prodigal
son is traditionally what it's called,
but that makes it sound like the first
son who leaves is the main character of
the story. And that's not really the
case. it's a primary character and then
the other son is another primary
character. And while the father is
necessary to the story, I don't think
we're intended to identify with the
father because in the overwhelming
majority of the interpretations, the
father is in the role of God because the
story is really about how we identify
the two sons and how we identify with
one of the two sons. uh it's about
salvation and some of the earliest
interpretations understand the prodigal
son to represent the Gentiles and they
are away from God's people and they are
you know gallivanting around with pigs
that's supposed to be a symbol of the
gentile world and then this is about the
Gentiles finally being given the gospel
and certain Gentiles recognizing its
power and coming into the gospel and
then the son who has been there all
along. The Jewish people is annoyed
about that. And so the story may be a
lesson about forgiveness to the
Gentiles. Others understand both sons to
be Christians. So what if there are
Christians who have gone away from the
gospel and then repent and return? Are
other Christians upset with them? There
are a variety of different ways to
understand this. But if you want to read
yourself into the role of the father,
you're reading yourself into the role of
God. And note what the father does. The
father acquiesces to the son's demands.
The father makes no demands of his own.
The father puts no conditions on the
child's return. The father does not send
messengers or anyone after the son to
chase them down. And if you want to put
yourself in the role of the father, you
must be putting yourself in a role that
demands unconditional love and patience
and longsuffering just like God is
represented in many parts of the Bible
as having. So I think to say, well, if
you look at the prodigal son, this means
you need to show me more respect or
things like that. There aren't a lot of
parables in the New Testament where you
read yourself into one of the roles so
that you can arrogate more rights or
authority or privileges to yourself.
Usually, if you're finding yourself in a
parable, you have things being demanded
of you. And I think that's true of this,
even though I would also say it kind of
reverses the rhetorical point of the
story and the direction of the
rhetorical message. So, I think that is
an inappropriate and an inaccurate
attempt to leverage the parable of the
prodigal son or as most scholars call it
today, the parable of the two sons. Hope
that's somewhat helpful.
